sections.h2: Which Franklin County offices do I deal with on a tax bill?
sections.html:
Two Franklin County offices touch your bill. Billing and collecting belong to the Tax Commissioner. Appraisal and exemption approval belong to the Board of Tax Assessors. Neither sets the rate: county commissioners and the school board do.

According to the tax office, the money pays for the following.

  • County government operations and the public schools.
  • Building and repairing public buildings and bridges.
  • Courts, the county jail and law enforcement.
  • County roads and fire protection.
  • Public health and sanitation.

Find the Tax Commissioner at 1221 Hull Avenue in Carnesville, the county seat; mail goes to PO Box 100, Carnesville, GA 30521. Phone the office at 706-384-3455 any weekday during those hours. For value, exemption or return questions, dial the Tax Assessor at 706-384-4896.

sections.h2: How does Franklin County arrive at the amount I owe?
sections.html:
Forty percent of the house's market value becomes the assessed value. Exemptions are taken from it and the millage rate is applied to the rest, a mill being $1 for each $1,000. Your bill lists both figures.

A buyer or an owner who changed the property sends the assessor form PT-50r between January 1 and April 1, and skipping it costs 10 percent of the omitted value plus interest. Owners with no change from the prior year may skip it.

sections.h2: Which Franklin County tax dates and rates should a seller know?
sections.html:
These rows pull together the dates and rates most sellers ask about, all drawn from the tax office and the county site.

Franklin County property tax basics (Franklin County Tax Office and Franklin County government pages)
ItemWhat the county says
Bills dueNormally November 15
Interest after the due date1 percent per month
Added penalty10 percent, if still unpaid at day 90
Assessment appeal window45 days after the notice
Homestead and return filingJanuary 1 to April 1
Mobile home return and permitOn or before May 1
Tax salesA first Tuesday, at the courthouse

Homesteaded property owing under $500 is spared the 10 percent penalty.

sections.h2: What does a late payment trigger in Franklin County?
sections.html:
After November 15 the clock starts: 1 percent monthly interest, then the 10 percent surcharge at 90 days. The fifa, or execution, is then filed with the Clerk of Superior Court. Anyone can read it, and credit bureaus may pull it; the tax office says it has no say over how they use it.

Only full payment of the delinquent taxes releases the lien. Failing that, the tax commissioner, who doubles as ex-officio sheriff, can levy on the property and auction it, a step the office calls its last resort.

If a bill is open when you sell, call 706-384-3455 for the amount owed through your closing date.

sections.h2: Where does a Franklin County value dispute go?
sections.html:
The notice carries a date, and you have 45 days counting from it. The assessors review the value again and send you a decision. Should they stand by their number, the Board of Equalization hears the dispute next, and Superior Court is open after that on written notice to the assessors.

Arbitration can replace the equalization hearing. An appeal can raise taxability, value or uniformity among comparable parcels. The tax rate itself cannot be appealed here, since it is set by other bodies.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can lower a Franklin County bill?
sections.html:
One application with the Tax Assessor starts the exemption, and it continues yearly until the owner changes or a different type is sought. Ownership and occupancy count as of January 1. The county exemptions page and the tax office FAQ name April 1 as the last day to file, but one older page on the tax office site says March 1, so file early and have the assessor confirm.

  • Standard homestead: $2,000 subtracted from assessed value (the county page's figure).
  • Age 65 and older, local exemption: $20,000 against all taxes on the homestead.
  • Age 62 and older, floating exemption: tied to natural increases in value, with an income cap of $30,000.
  • Disabled veterans: $100,896, and a surviving spouse who has not remarried or minor children can keep it.
  • Deferral program: for homeowners aged 62 or over earning no more than $15,000 gross, payment can wait until the property changes hands or the deferred balance and interest climb to 85 percent of its value.

Final eligibility rests with the assessors; a denied applicant gets notice and an appeal path.

sections.h2: What is different for farmland and timber in Franklin County?
sections.html:
Land programs carry weight in a county with about 90 people per square mile. Qualifying farm property can be assessed at 30 percent rather than 40. Under conservation use, farm and timber land is valued at its current use rather than market value, but the owner signs a covenant to keep it in that use for ten years. File for conservation use with the assessors by April 1 and pay a $25 recording fee.

A broken covenant costs twice the taxes saved, except after death or condemnation (no penalty) or medically shown illness or foreclosure (one year of savings). A sale does not trigger the penalty when the buyer signs the covenant and keeps the same use.

Timber standing on the land is untaxed until it is cut or sold; then it is valued at 100 percent of market. A mobile or modular home is taxed as personal property each year, with its return and location permit due by May 1 and the year's tax paid first.

sections.h2: What else does the Franklin County tax office handle that a seller may meet?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner also runs the county tag office in the Court House Annex at 1221 Hull Avenue, open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. Plan tag renewals for the 30 days leading up to the owner's birthday; a vehicle you just bought must be registered within 30 days. The office warns that some private websites charge a fee on top of the renewal; the official route is the Georgia Department of Revenue site.

Tax paid in error can be refunded on a written claim to the board of commissioners made within three years. The office says refunds rest on errors, and a disagreement over value is handled through the appeal process instead. Personal property owners file a PT-50p return every year by April 1, whether or not anything changed.

You may also see a Homeowner's Tax Relief Grant line mentioned in older materials. The tax office notes the state stopped funding that credit after the 2009 tax year, so do not expect it on a current bill.

sections.h2: How does a Franklin County tax sale work, and can the owner redeem?
sections.html:
Auctions are called for a first Tuesday outside the courthouse and advertised in the Franklin County Citizen every week for a month beforehand. Bidding starts at what the parcel owes in taxes, fees and interest.

Redemption stays open for twelve months, to the owner, creditors or other parties with an interest. The price is the buyer's purchase amount, any taxes the buyer paid since, special assessments, and a premium: 20 percent for the first year or portion, then 10 percent for each added year or portion. The buyer cannot take possession, collect rent or improve the property in that period. The county tells readers to take foreclosure questions to an attorney.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about the Franklin County market?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate for Franklin County is 25,948 people, up 10.8 percent from April 2020, across 261.35 square miles. The county holds 11,475 housing units, and owners occupy 77.2 percent of the lived-in ones. Builders took out 142 permits in 2025. Value of the median owner-occupied home: $179,000 (2020 to 2024). Median household income: $53,046. Share of residents 65 and older: 19.6 percent.

With so many older residents, the senior exemptions above reach a sizable share of owners. Monthly owner costs have a median of $432 without a mortgage and $1,432 with one, and median gross rent is $844. Employers numbered 515 in 2023, with 7,184 employees between them, and 2022 retail sales reached $516,981,000.

faqs.q: When must Franklin County taxes be paid?
faqs.a: By November 15 in the usual case. Late bills add 1 percent interest a month, plus a 10 percent penalty at the 90-day mark.

faqs.q: Who explains my Franklin County property value?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor, 706-384-4896. The Tax Commissioner, 706-384-3455, handles billing and payment only.

faqs.q: How long do Franklin County owners have to contest a value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the notice's date. Start with the assessors; the equalization board or arbitration is next, and Superior Court is last.

faqs.q: Does Franklin County give older homeowners a break?
faqs.a: Yes. Franklin County's exemptions page prints a local $20,000 break for homeowners 65 and older, separate state breaks at ages 62 and 65 that carry income limits, and a deferral option with a $15,000 gross income ceiling.

faqs.q: Can an owner redeem after a Franklin County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, for twelve months, if you pay the buyer the redemption amount the county itemizes, with a 20 percent premium in year one. The tax deed holder gets no possession during that year.
